title: 1  Introduction
text:
2 Welcome to Python!
Python is a modern programming language that is especially well-suited for beginners. It is easy to understand and used in many fields – from data analysis to web development.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
2.1 Learning goals of this chapter
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - write simple Python programs, - display text on the screen, - define and use basic variables.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
2.2 Your first program
The first steps in any new programming language are always the same. We start by printing the words ‘Hello World’. For this, we use the print() command:

print("Hello World!")

Hello World!


What happens here? - print() is a function that displays something on the screen. - The text "Hello World!" is shown. - Texts (also called “strings”) are always enclosed in quotation marks.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
2.3 Variables – Names for values
Variables are like labeled drawers: they store information under a name.

name = "Ms. Miller"
age = 32

You can use these variables to create dynamic output:

print(name + " is " + str(age) + " years old.")

Ms. Miller is 32 years old.


Note that here you are trying to output both a number and text. Therefore, we use the str() function to convert the number into text.






Tip✏️ Exercise: Greeting with age





Write a program that greets you with your name:
Hello Ms. Miller!
Tip: In Python, you can concatenate text using +. Remember that strings must be in quotation marks.






CautionSolution






my_name = "Your name here"
print("Hello " + my_name + "!")

Hello Your name here!





Extend your program so that it greets you and also states your age:
Hello Ms. Miller!
You are 32 years old.
Tip: Use multiple print() statements or concatenate the text.






CautionSolution






name = "Ms. Miller"
age = 32

print("Hello " + name + "!")
print("You are " + str(age) + " years old.")

Hello Ms. Miller!
You are 32 years old.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.1 Learning Objectives of This Chapter
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
distinguish the most important data types,
work with numbers and text,
perform simple calculations and print outputs.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.2 Introduction
Python has various data types. These describe what kind of data you store in variables. This is important because many operations—like +—can behave differently depending on the data type:

+ with numbers means addition,
+ with text means concatenation (joining together).

So before we move on to more complex programs, we should understand which data types exist and how to use them.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.3 The Most Important Data Types
Here are the basic data types in Python:



Type
Example
Meaning




int
10
Integer (whole number)


float
3.14
Decimal number (floating point)


str
"Hello"
Text (string)


bool
True, False
Boolean (yes/no)



You can check the type of a variable using the type() function:

value = 42
print(type(value))  # Output: <class 'int'>

<class 'int'>

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.4 Difference Between int and float
In Python, we distinguish between integers (int) and floating point numbers (float):

int stands for “integer” – whole numbers like 1, 0, -10
float stands for “floating point number” – numbers with decimal places like 3.14, 0.5, -2.0


a = 10       # int
b = 2.5      # float

print("a:", a, "| Type:", type(a))
print("b:", b, "| Type:", type(b))

a: 10 | Type: <class 'int'>
b: 2.5 | Type: <class 'float'>








Important





This distinction is important: some operations behave slightly differently depending on the data type.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.5 What Are Booleans (bool)?
A Boolean is a truth value: it can only have two possible states:

True
False

These values show up in situations like:

Is the temperature above 30 °C?
Does the file have a certain name?
Is the list empty?


is_sunny = True
has_umbrella = False

print("Sunny:", is_sunny)
print("Has umbrella?", has_umbrella)
print("Type of 'is_sunny':", type(is_sunny))

Sunny: True
Has umbrella? False
Type of 'is_sunny': <class 'bool'>


Booleans are especially useful in conditions and comparisons, which you will learn more about in Chapter 3.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.6 Doing Math with Numbers
Python can be used like a calculator:



Operator
Description




+, -
Addition / Subtraction


*, /
Multiplication / Division


//, %
Integer Division / Remainder


**
Exponentiation




a = 10
b = 3

print("Addition:", a + b)
print("Subtraction:", a - b)
print("Multiplication:", a * b)
print("Exponentiation:", a**b)
print("Division:", a / b)
print("Integer Division:", a // b)
print("Remainder:", a % b)

Addition: 13
Subtraction: 7
Multiplication: 30
Exponentiation: 1000
Division: 3.3333333333333335
Integer Division: 3
Remainder: 1








Note





// means integer division: the result is rounded down. Alternatively, % performs integer division and returns the remainder.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.7 Working with Text
Text (strings) can be combined:

first_name = "Anna"
last_name = "Example"
print("Welcome, " + first_name + " " + last_name + "!")

Welcome, Anna Example!


If you want to combine text and numbers, you must convert the number to a string:

points = 95
print("You scored " + str(points) + " points.")

You scored 95 points.

title: 2  Understanding Data Types
text:
2.8 Type Conversion (Typecasting)
Sometimes you need to convert a value from one data type to another— e.g., a number to a string so it can be printed.
This is called typecasting. Here are the most common functions:



Function
Description
Example




str()
Number → Text
str(42) → "42"


int()
Text/number → Integer
int("10") → 10


float()
Text/number → Float
float("3.14") → 3.14




# Example: display a number as text
points = 100
print("You scored " + str(points) + " points.")

# Example: convert string to number and do a calculation
input_value = "3.5"
value = float(input_value) * 2
print("Double the value:", value)

You scored 100 points.
Double the value: 7.0


When converting, make sure the content is appropriate – int("abc") will cause an error.






TipExercise: Age in Days





Calculate how old a person is in days.

age_years = 32
days = age_years * 365
print("You are approximately " + str(days) + " days old.")

You are approximately 11680 days old.


Tip: Remember to convert the number to a string when printing it.






CautionSolution






age = 32
days = age * 365
print("You are approximately " + str(days) + " days old.")

You are approximately 11680 days old.

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
text:
3.1 Learning Objectives of This Chapter
Programs often need to make decisions – for example, based on user input or a specific value. Similarly, certain actions need to be repeated multiple times.
Python provides two key elements for this:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
text:
Formulate conditions using if, elif, and else,
Use comparison operators (==, <, !=, …),
Implement loops with while and for.

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
3  Decisions and Loops
text:
3.3 Comparison Operators



Expression
Meaning




a == b
equal


a != b
not equal


a < b
less than


a > b
greater than


a <= b
less than or equal


a >= b
greater than or equal

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
text:
3.4 Repetitions with while

counter = 0

while counter < 5:
    print("Counter is:", counter)
    counter += 1

Counter is: 0
Counter is: 1
Counter is: 2
Counter is: 3
Counter is: 4








Important





Make sure to include a stopping condition – otherwise, the loop will run endlessly!

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
text:
3.5 Loops with for and range()
If you want to repeat something a specific number of times, use for with range():

for i in range(5):
    print("Iteration:", i)

Iteration: 0
Iteration: 1
Iteration: 2
Iteration: 3
Iteration: 4


Set a custom start and end value:

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

1
2
3
4
5

title: 3  Decisions and Loops
text:
3.6 What exactly does range() do?
The range() function creates a sequence of numbers that can be iterated over with a for loop.

Variants:
range(5)
➡️ yields: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (starts at 0, ends before 5)
range(2, 6)
➡️ yields: 2, 3, 4, 5 (starts at 2, ends before 6)
range(1, 10, 2)
➡️ yields: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (step size = 2)
range() does not create a real list, but a so-called “range object” that behaves like a list.

Use a for loop to print the numbers from 1 to 10.

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.1 What is a List?
Until now, you’ve stored individual values in variables. But what if you want to store a whole list of numbers, names, or values at once?
For that, Python has lists. In this chapter, you’ll also learn how to iterate over lists using for loops.
A list is an ordered collection of values of the same data type.
names = ["Ali", "Bente", "Carlos"]
grades = [1.7, 2.3, 1.3, 2.0]
You access elements using square brackets:
print(names[0])   # first element
print(grades[-1]) # last element

Ali
2.0

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.2 Slicing Lists
With slicing, you can extract specific parts of a list. You specify where the slice starts and where it ends (the end value is not included):

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
print(numbers[1:4])  # Output: [20, 30, 40]

[20, 30, 40]



Syntax: list[start:stop]

start: index where slicing starts (inclusive)
stop: index where it ends (exclusive)
You can omit the start index: [:3] → first to third element
Or omit the stop index: [3:] → from fourth element to end
Full copy: [:]


print(numbers[:3])   # [10, 20, 30]
print(numbers[3:])   # [40, 50, 60]
print(numbers[:])    # full copy

[10, 20, 30]
[40, 50, 60]
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]








Note





You can also use negative indices (-1 is the last element):

print(numbers[-3:])  # [40, 50, 60]

[40, 50, 60]

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.3 Iterating Over Lists
You can use a for loop to iterate over each element in a list:

names = ["Ali", "Bente", "Carlos"]

for name in names:
    print("Hello", name + "!")

Hello Ali!
Hello Bente!
Hello Carlos!

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.4 Extension: Conditional Output
You can use if statements inside the loop to filter:

temperatures = [14.2, 17.5, 19.0, 21.3, 18.4]

for t in temperatures:
    if t > 18:
        print(t, "is a warm day")

19.0 is a warm day
21.3 is a warm day
18.4 is a warm day

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.5 Calculating the Average
Python provides useful functions such as sum() and len():

grades = [1.7, 2.3, 1.3, 2.0]

average = sum(grades) / len(grades)
print("Average grade:", round(average, 2))

Average grade: 1.82

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.6 Expanding Lists: .append()
Sometimes you don’t know the list elements beforehand — you can add new values later:

names = []

names.append("Ali")
names.append("Bente")

print(names)

['Ali', 'Bente']








Note





The .append() method adds a new value to the end of the list.

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.7 Nested Loops
If you’re working with multidimensional data — such as a table with several rows — you can nest loops:

weekdays = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
hours = [1, 2, 3]

for day in weekdays:
    for hour in hours:
        print(f"{day}, hour {hour}")

Mon, hour 1
Mon, hour 2
Mon, hour 3
Tue, hour 1
Tue, hour 2
Tue, hour 3
Wed, hour 1
Wed, hour 2
Wed, hour 3


This results in:
Mon, hour 1
Mon, hour 2
Mon, hour 3
Tue, hour 1
...

title: 4  Storing Multiple Values
text:
4.8 Sorting Lists
With sorted(), you can sort lists alphabetically or numerically:

names = ["Zoe", "Anna", "Ben"]
sorted_names = sorted(names)

print(sorted_names)

['Anna', 'Ben', 'Zoe']








Important





The original list remains unchanged.
If you want to modify the list directly, you can use:

names.sort()

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.1 Learning Goals of This Chapter
Imagine you need to perform a specific calculation multiple times in your program. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, you can bundle it into a function.
Functions are a key tool to make code:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
create your own functions using def,
pass parameters and use return values,
apply functions effectively in programs.

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.2 Defining a Function
A function consists of the following parts:

Definition with def
Function name
Parameters in parentheses (optional)
Indentation for the function body
(optional) return statement

Example:

def hello(name="Guest"):
    greeting = "Hello " + name + "!"
    return greeting

Let’s start with the first keyword. Functions are defined with def and can be called as often as you like:

def greeting():
    print("Hello and welcome!")

It only runs when you call it:

greeting()

Hello and welcome!

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.3 Passing Parameters
Functions can receive input values (parameters):

def greeting(name):
    print("Hello", name + "!")

greeting("Alex")

Hello Alex!

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.4 Return Values with return
A function can also return a value:

def square(number):
    return number * number

result = square(5)
print(result)

25

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.5 Example: Conversions

Euro to US Dollar

def euro_to_usd(amount_euro):
    exchange_rate = 1.09
    return amount_euro * exchange_rate

print("20 € is", euro_to_usd(20), "US dollars.")

20 € is 21.8 US dollars.








TipTask: Greeting with Name





Create a function greet(name) that uses the name in a greeting text:
Hello Fatima, nice to see you!






CautionSolution






def greet(name):
    print("Hello", name + ", nice to see you!")

greet("Fatima")

Hello Fatima, nice to see you!














TipTask: Temperature Conversion





Write a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit:
Formula: [ F = C + 32 ]






CautionSolution






def celsius_to_fahrenheit(c):
    return c * 1.8 + 32

print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(20))

68.0

title: 5  Reusable Code with Functions
text:
5.6 Parameters with Default Values
You can assign default values to parameters. That way, the function can be called even without providing a value:

def greeting(name="Guest"):
    print("Hello", name + "!")

greeting()         # Hello Guest!
greeting("Maria")  # Hello Maria!

Hello Guest!
Hello Maria!








Noteprint() vs. return





These two concepts are often confused:



Expression
Meaning




print()
displays text on the screen


return
gives a value back to the caller



Example:

def double(x):
    return x * 2

# Make the output visible
print(double(5))  # Output: 10

10

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
6.1 Learning Goals of This Chapter
Programs often work not only with user input but also with text files – for example, to save or load data.
Python offers simple functions to:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
open files using open(),
read content from text files,
write text into files,
work safely and easily using with blocks.

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
6.2 Reading a File

# Example: Reading a file
with open("01-daten/beispiel.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
    print(content)

This is a sample file.
It contains several lines of text.
Each line can be read individually.



"r" stands for read.
with ensures that the file is automatically closed after reading.
read() reads the entire content of the file as a string.

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
6.3 Reading Line by Line

with open("01-daten/beispiel.txt", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        print("Line:", line.strip())

Line: This is a sample file.
Line: It contains several lines of text.
Line: Each line can be read individually.








Note





.strip() removes whitespace and line breaks at the beginning and end.









TipTask: Read a File





Suppose there is a file gruesse.txt with the following content:
Hallo Anna
Guten Morgen Ben
Willkommen Carla
Write a program that reads each line one by one and outputs it using print(...).






CautionSolution






with open("01-daten/gruesse.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

Hallo Anna
Guten Morgen Ben
Willkommen Carla

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
6.4 Writing to a File

with open("ausgabe.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("This is a new line.\n")
    file.write("And another one.")


"w" stands for write.
Caution: An existing file will be overwritten!

title: 6  Working with Files
section: 6.5 Writing Line by Line Using a Loop
text:
6.5 Writing Line by Line Using a Loop

data = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]

with open("obst.txt", "w") as f:
    for entry in data:
        f.write(entry + "\n")







Important





Each line ends with \n for a line break.









TipTask: Write a List to a File





Given a list of cities:
cities = ["Berlin", "Hamburg", "Munich"]

Write a program that writes each city to a new line in a file called cities.txt.







CautionSolution






cities = ["Berlin", "Hamburg", "Munich"]

with open("cities.txt", "w") as f:
    for city in cities:
        f.write(city + "\n")

title: 6  Working with Files
section: 6.6 Reading All Lines at Once with readlines()
text:
6.6 Reading All Lines at Once with readlines()
Instead of iterating over a file, you can read all lines at once as a list:

with open("01-daten/beispiel.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
    print(lines)

['This is a sample file.\n', 'It contains several lines of text.\n', 'Each line can be read individually.']








Important





Each line ends with \n, so post-processing with .strip() is often helpful:

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())

This is a sample file.
It contains several lines of text.
Each line can be read individually.

title: 6  Working with Files
text:
6.7 Closing Files Manually with close()
If you do not use a with block, you must close the file yourself – otherwise it stays open:

file = open("test.txt", "w")
file.write("This is a test.")
file.close()







Important





close() is important to ensure changes are saved and the file is not locked.
Recommendation: Always use with open(...), because Python will automatically close the file – even if an error occurs.
